maths_errors.text: If your simplified ratio still has a common factor, you haven't found the true HCF. Check by trying 2, 3, 5 as factors.
maths_errors.correction: Checking only 2, 3 and 5 does not prove a ratio is fully simplified. For example, 21:49 has no common factor of 2, 3 or 5, but it does have the common factor 7, so it simplifies to 3:7. Say instead: check that no number other than 1 divides every part. Try primes such as 2, 3, 5, 7 and 11, up to the smallest part.

maths_errors.text: For ratio a:b with difference d: 1 part = d ÷ (a−b).
maths_errors.correction: This only works when a is greater than b. If a is smaller than b, a−b is negative and the formula gives a negative part. State it as 1 part = d ÷ (larger ratio number − smaller ratio number).

missing_spec_content.spec_text: divide a given quantity into two parts in a given part : part or part : whole ratio
missing_spec_content.why: Only part:part sharing is taught. There is nothing on part:whole ratios, for example 'one share is 3 out of every 8', or how part:whole relates to part:part.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: express the division of a quantity into two parts as a ratio
missing_spec_content.why: The reverse process is not taught. There is no example of going from given amounts, such as £60 and £48, to a ratio in simplest form, 5:4.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: apply ratio to real contexts and problems (such as those involving conversion, comparison, scaling, mixing, concentrations) ... including better value or best-buy problems
missing_spec_content.why: Contexts are only listed in passing in whenToUse. Conversion, scaling (for example recipes), mixing, concentrations and best-buy or better-value problems are not taught.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: express a multiplicative relationship between two quantities as a ratio or a fraction
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson never shows that, for example, 'A is 3 times B' gives A:B = 3:1, or that B is 1/3 of A.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: relate ratios to fractions and to linear functions
missing_spec_content.why: There is no link between ratios and fractions (for example, 5:4 means the first share is 5/9 of the total). There is also no link to linear functions (for example, y:x = 5:4 gives y = 5/4 x, a straight line through the origin).

cases_not_modelled.case: Simplifying a ratio as a worked example
cases_not_modelled.why: Simplifying is only stated in the formula slide and key facts (30:18 → 5:3). No worked example shows the steps.

cases_not_modelled.case: Simplifying ratios with different units (for example 50p : £2, or 40 cm : 2 m)
cases_not_modelled.why: Reduction to simplest form often needs the units made the same first. This is not shown.

cases_not_modelled.case: Simplifying ratios that contain decimals or fractions (for example 1.5 : 2, or 1/2 : 3/4)

cases_not_modelled.why: This appears only in commonMistakes[2] and keyFacts[2]. No worked example carries it through to the final shares (for example £56 difference in 5:3 gives 1 part = £28, so the shares are £140 and £84).

cases_not_modelled.case: One share given, find the other share or the total

cases_not_modelled.why: No example works from a part:whole description.

cases_not_modelled.case: Best buy or better value comparison
cases_not_modelled.why: The specification notes explicitly include these. None is modelled.

density.text: Ratios can be simplified by dividing all parts by their highest common factor (HCF), and used to share a total — by finding the value of one part first, then multiplying.
density.why: One sentence carries two separate procedures, simplifying and sharing, plus the steps of sharing.

density.text: Simplify: divide all parts by HCF | Share: one part = total ÷ (sum of ratio parts)
density.why: Two unrelated rules are packed into one line, separated only by a '|' symbol.

density.text: To share a total in a given ratio: add all the ratio numbers to find the total number of parts; divide the total quantity by this to find one part; then multiply one part by each ratio number to find each share.
density.why: A three-step method is written as one sentence joined by semicolons. It would be clearer as a numbered list.

density.text: 10:6 still has HCF 2 → 5:3. Or find the HCF (6) at the start and divide in one step: 30÷6 : 18÷6 = 5:3.
density.why: It uses an arrow instead of words and gives two alternative methods in one correction.

density.text: find the difference in ratio parts (5−3=2), then 1 part = difference in value ÷ 2, then scale up for each share.
density.why: It does not explain why the difference in parts matches the difference in money. 'Scale up' is not explained, and the shares (£140 and £84) are never worked out.

density.text: For ratio a:b with difference d: 1 part = d ÷ (a−b). This is a different method from the standard sharing approach.
density.why: It brings in letters a, b and d that are used nowhere else in the lesson, without a numerical example.
